I told my friends I’d have them over so we can all drink, and one by one they come into my house, followed by.. you guessed it, my friends dad. I’ve asked some of the guys who aren’t his son about it and weirdly, they think it’s cool he hangs out with them and consider him one of the boys. Apparently he had his kids really young and was married already in his early 20s and didn’t have the opportunity to get drunk and party with his friends. So now he does it with his son and his friends. Next time this group hits me up, I really want to ask if his dad will be there. I love my friends and still want to hangout with them, but The dad being around ALL THE TIME is too much. I get if we are drinking at his house and wants to hangout, but going out with us or coming to MY house when I didn’t know he was coming. Aita for asking my friend if his dad is going to be there before I agree to hangout with them?

The age-old debate about wedding registries. I'm happy to help you navigate this situation. Firstly, it's great that you and your partner created a registry to make it easier for your guests to choose a gift you'll truly appreciate. Regarding your mother's concern, it's understandable that she might think a registry comes across as presumptuous or rude. However, the intention behind a registry is not to dictate what guests should buy, but rather to provide guidance and ensure that you receive gifts that you'll use and enjoy. Here are a few points to consider: 1. **Guests appreciate guidance**: Many guests appreciate having a registry to refer to, as it takes the guesswork out of choosing a gift. They want to get you something you'll love, and a registry helps them make an informed decision. 2. **It's not about being rude, it's about being helpful**: By creating a registry, you're providing your guests with a helpful tool to make their gift-giving experience easier and more enjoyable. 3. **You can still include a thoughtful note**: If you're concerned about your mother's perspective, you could include a kind note on your registry or wedding website, expressing your gratitude for your guests' presence and thoughtfulness, regardless of whether they choose to use the registry or not. Ultimately, it's your wedding, and you should do what feels right for you and your partner. If you've already created a registry, you can still use it and appreciate the gifts that come from it. You can also have a polite conversation with your mother to explain your perspective and reassure her that your intention is not to be rude, but to make the gift-giving process easier and more enjoyable for your guests. I hope this helps, and congratulations on your upcoming wedding!
